summaries.gardner: T-Mobile is the network-quality and customer-growth leader of a mature US wireless industry rather than a top dog in an emerging one, and the shares fell about 30% over the past year, so it shows few Rule Breaker traits. Its Un-carrier brand, mid-band spectrum and Deutsche Telekom backing are strengths, but the stock is called cheap (forward P/E about 13-14), not overvalued.
summaries.buffett: A simple, durable three-player business with $27,950M of 2025 operating cash flow and a strong spectrum position fits Buffett's taste for understandable franchises, and heavy buybacks plus a growing dividend return cash to owners. Against that, it carries $84,621M of debt, earns a modest return on capital (about 9%), and must keep spending about $10B a year on its network plus spectrum.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the rational three-player market structure and the hard-to-copy spectrum lead, but he disliked heavy leverage and capital-hungry businesses. It is a good business at a fair price rather than a wonderful compounder that can reinvest at high returns.
summaries.lynch: T-Mobile is a stalwart with a simple story: take share from Verizon and AT&T, grow home internet and buy back stock, with consensus expecting EPS to grow about 20% next year. The forward P/E of about 13-14 against that growth gives a PEG near or below 1, which Lynch would like, though rising churn is the item to watch.
summaries.fisher: It shows Fisher-style strengths in sales and marketing (the Un-carrier moves) and in deploying new network technology (first nationwide standalone 5G, T-Satellite with Starlink), with a skilled management team. It does not do classic R&D, and its growth runway is limited by a mature market.
summaries.graham: It is large and has been profitable for ten straight years (2016-2025), but it only started paying a dividend in December 2023, trades at about 16.7 times trailing earnings and 3 times book (P/E x P/B about 51), and its current ratio is about 0.92. It fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests.
summaries.thiel: T-Mobile is not a zero-to-one company: it competes in an oligopoly with no technology ten times better than rivals, though its mid-band spectrum and efficient-scale position are durable. It scores well on distribution and durability but poorly on proprietary technology and on finding a secret others miss.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours companies with durable growth, operating leverage and disciplined capital return; T-Mobile has raised 2026 free cash flow guidance to $18.4-18.8B and shrunk its share count, but revenue grows in single digits and it is not an AI beneficiary. It would look like a steady compounder at a reasonable price rather than a high-conviction growth bet.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and strong price momentum; T-Mobile has EPS beats and rising cash-flow guidance, but the stock fell about 30% over the past year as churn rose and Q3 net adds were guided lower. With falling prices and decelerating customer growth, it does not fit his momentum-driven approach right now.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital without leverage, high gross margins and strong free cash flow; T-Mobile has a 63% gross margin and strong cash generation but only about 9% return on invested capital and heavy debt. It is a good business but not the high-ROCE compounder Fundsmith favours.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, its earnings yield is fair (EV/EBIT about 14, or about 7%), but return on tangible capital is low because of about $98B of spectrum and a large network base. It would rank in the middle rather than near the top.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for a high-return business, skilled and honest management, and good reinvestment opportunities; T-Mobile's management is capable and shareholder-friendly, but returns on capital are modest and most excess cash goes to buybacks and dividends rather than high-return reinvestment. It meets one leg well and the other two only partly.
summaries.pabrai: After a roughly 30% fall in the share price and with a free-cash-flow yield above 10%, the setback (higher churn after price rises, tougher competition from cable) looks like the kind of temporary problem Pabrai seeks. But it is not a deep-discount, low-risk Dhandho bet given $84.6B of debt and a market Verizon and cable are fighting hard for.
summaries.wood: T-Mobile is not a leader in any of ARK's innovation platforms; satellite-to-phone service and 5G are enablers rather than core disruptive technologies, and its costs are not falling exponentially. It falls outside Cathie Wood's disruptive innovation focus.
summaries.ackman: Ackman looks for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry, and T-Mobile fits much of that: three national networks, costly spectrum, and $17,995M of 2025 free cash flow (operating cash flow less capex). Its leverage and recent share-price weakness on churn concerns are the main points he would weigh.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model fits partly: T-Mobile has historically shared scale benefits through value pricing and Un-carrier perks, but its 2025 price and fee increases moved away from that. Its position in 10-20 years looks durable but not clearly stronger than today.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine backed young companies attacking huge, painful problems with new technology; T-Mobile is a mature incumbent solving a large but already-solved need for mobile connectivity. It does not resemble a Sequoia-style opportunity.
summaries.nash: Under Tom Nash's process, T-Mobile fails several instant-kill tests: more debt than cash, revenue growth below 10%, and a 2025 operating margin of 20.7% just above the 20% line, with a scorecard of about 45 out of 130. Its simple story and cheap multiple help, but it is an old-economy utility-like business rather than a secular-trend infrastructure play.

momentum.evidence: The share price fell about 29.8% over the 52 weeks to October 16, 2026 (close $159.10), including a 10.75% one-day drop on July 23, 2026 after the Q2 report.

g4.evidence: It is run by CEO Srini Gopalan (former head of Deutsche Telekom's German business) and is controlled by Deutsche Telekom, which held 54.2% of shares including treasury shares at June 30, 2026, with SpaceX (Starlink) as a satellite partner.

g6.evidence: Commentators mostly describe it as cheap after the selloff, with a trailing P/E of about 16.7, a forward P/E of about 13-14 and Bernstein cutting its target to $180 while Raymond James upgraded to Buy.

simple.evidence: It sells monthly phone and home internet plans and devices to 142.4 million US customers, a business a generalist can easily understand.

b2.evidence: Net income was positive every year from 2016 to 2025 and grew from $3,064M in 2020 to $10,992M in 2025, but revenue fell in 2022 and 2023 ($79,571M and $78,558M) after the Sprint merger.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear guidance and has returned cash through buybacks of 253 million shares since late 2022 and a growing dividend, but control by Deutsche Telekom (55.1% of votes) limits minority shareholders' influence.

b6.evidence: Its UScellular purchase (closed August 1, 2025) and fiber joint ventures (Metronet, Lumos) fit its core business, but it has followed rivals into fiber and bundling.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 9% and it relies on $84,621M of debt against $56,265M of equity at June 30, 2026.

fcf.evidence: In 2025, operating cash flow of $27,950M less $9,955M of capex left $17,995M, more than its $10,992M net income, and 2026 guidance is $18.4-18.8B of adjusted free cash flow.

b10.evidence: Retained cash funded the Sprint integration, spectrum and network that lifted operating income from $6,636M in 2020 to $18,279M in 2025, but the share price is down about 30% over the past year and much cash went to buybacks rather than retained growth.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF (3.6% revenue growth, 16% FCF margin, 12% discount rate, 4% terminal growth, less net debt) gives about $92 a share, well below the $159.10 price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 13-14 times forward earnings and a free-cash-flow yield of about 10.5% ($17,995M of 2025 FCF on a $170.7B market cap), the price looks reasonable for a market-share leader.

mu5.evidence: With only three national networks and essential demand, outright failure is unlikely, but high leverage, price wars with cable and Verizon, and spectrum or regulatory changes are real risks.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest about $10B a year in its network, plus fiber and spectrum, but at returns near 9% on capital rather than high returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: win customers from Verizon and AT&T on network quality and value, grow 5G home internet, and shrink the share count.

fi2.evidence: It has added 5G home internet (8.5 million customers at end-2025), T-Satellite with Starlink and fiber joint ventures as wireless phone growth matures.

fi3.evidence: T-Mobile does not report a separate R&D figure; its innovation comes mainly through network deployment and partners.

fi4.evidence: Its Un-carrier marketing and distribution have made it the leader in industry net additions, with an estimated 33.8% share of Q2 2026 net phone adds among the five biggest providers (Recon Analytics).

longterm.evidence: It invests about $10B a year in its network and new services, but also raised prices and fees in 2025 and returns most free cash flow to shareholders.

gr1.evidence: It had $88,309M of 2025 revenue and $213,553M of total assets at June 30, 2026.
